did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 22 opens with the prophetic formula, “The word of the LORD came to me, saying,” presenting Ezekiel as a messenger receiving a direct message from the LORD.
Did you know? Ezekiel is commanded to “judge” Jerusalem and proclaim all her abominations. Jerusalem is called the “city of bloodshed” because of the bloodshed that took place within it.
Did you know? Jerusalem’s sins are described in two main areas: bloodshed and idolatry. The city is also portrayed as defiling itself with its idols.
Did you know? The chapter places special responsibility on Israel’s leaders. They are described as using their power to shed blood, meaning that the leadership itself was involved in injustice.

Did you know? Alongside violence and idolatry, the chapter details the mistreatment of vulnerable groups: the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. In this way, the treatment of the vulnerable is presented as a central moral measure.

Did you know? Desecrating the Sabbath and profaning holy things appear in the chapter as part of the same system of corruption. Violations of sacred matters are presented alongside social and moral injustices.

Did you know? Ezekiel lists among Jerusalem’s sins slander, idolatry, incest, bribery, charging interest, and oppression. This broad list emphasizes that the city’s corruption affected social, religious, and legal life.

Did you know? The house of Israel is compared to a mixture of metals and dross in a furnace. In the chapter, the image of the furnace describes the gathering of the people in Jerusalem and their exposure to the fire of judgment.

Did you know? The land itself is described as “not cleansed” and as receiving no rain on the day of wrath. Thus, impurity is attributed not only to the people but also to the land where their deeds took place.

Did you know? The LORD says that He looked for someone who would rebuild the wall and stand in the breach before Him on behalf of the land, but He found no one. This image highlights the absence of a leader or mediator willing to act to prevent the land’s destruction.
